cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A 50-year-old Indian woman with diabetes and hypertension presented with right upper abdominal discomfort, loss of appetite, and low-grade fever. She denied jaundice.  
On examination, she had hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right hypochondrium.  
Laboratory studies showed normal liver-function tests. Serological tests for amoebiasis and hydatid disease were negative. A chest radiograph was normal.  
Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 11 × 7.5 × 11.2 cm predominantly anechoic, thick-walled lesion arising from the inferior surface of the liver, with low-level internal echoes and a homogeneous echogenic area in its superolateral portion. The gallbladder was not visualized separately; other abdominal viscera were normal.  
Aspiration of the lesion yielded turbid fluid, but the lesion persisted despite repeated aspirations and antibiotic therapy.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, lobulated cystic lesion with a solid component in its superior part, abutting the colon and duodenum. The lesion was interpreted as an infected non-parasitic cyst.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 45-year-old man presented with a three-week history of a tender, slow-growing left axillary lump and a low-grade fever (37.5–38°C) for one week. His medical history was notable for hypertension—treated with lacidipine, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide—and a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass performed two years earlier, after which he lost 112 kg (BMI from 64.6 to 28 kg/m2). He smoked 30 cigarettes daily and took vitamin (A, D, E, B complex), calcium, cholecalciferol, and iron supplements. There was no personal or family history of autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disease. On examination, he had a tender, non-mobile, 3 × 4 cm lymph node in the left axilla; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies—including a complete blood count, ESR, liver and renal panels, autoantibodies (ANA, RF), complement levels, inflammatory markers, thyroid function, and serologies for a broad spectrum of viral and parasitic pathogens—were all normal or negative. A thoracoabdominal CT scan was unremarkable except for the axillary lymphadenopathy. A biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate. An investigation for mycobacteria was negative.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 4-year-old African-American girl presented with a several-day history of cough, nasal congestion, intermittent fever, severe intermittent abdominal pain, and bloody stools. Her medical history included sickle cell disease, ulcerative colitis, and autoimmune hepatitis, treated with hydroxyurea, mesalamine, and azathioprine. On examination, she had clusters of 2–7 mm hemorrhagic vesicles on her palms, knees, and soles, and a tender, swollen right knee. Laboratory evaluation showed a C-reactive protein level of 31.1 mg/dL, leukocytosis (25.5 × 10^3 cells/µL), and anemia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, hematocrit 18.7%). Bacterial and viral cultures of vesicle fluid were negative. Four months earlier, she had a similar episode attributed to a sickle cell crisis versus a flare of ulcerative colitis; biopsy at that time revealed a neutrophilic panniculitis. During the current admission, a repeat skin biopsy showed subcorneal and subepidermal edema and a dense acute neutrophilic infiltrate extending into adipose tissue and septa. Direct immunofluorescence of the lesion was negative.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 40-year-old man presented with 1 week of difficulty voiding and was catheterized for urinary retention. Ultrasonography revealed a large prostatic mass, and his prostate-specific antigen level was 0.62 ng/mL (normal <4.0). He denied pain, fever, or abdominal distension. Physical examination was unremarkable, and complete blood count, routine chemistries, and tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA-125, SCC antigen, CYFRA) were all within normal limits. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged prostate with palpable nodules and an ill-defined border. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a heterogeneous prostatic mass. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a 5.5-cm heterogeneous lesion in the right prostate lobe, and cystoscopy raised suspicion for bladder invasion. Positron emission tomography–CT and colonoscopy suggested rectal invasion. A provisional diagnosis of prostatic sarcoma was made, and a transrectal needle biopsy was performed. The biopsy result was interpreted as either prostatic stromal sarcoma or prostatic stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 13-year-old boy with T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia receiving maintenance therapy (daily 6-mercaptopurine, weekly methotrexate, monthly vincristine and dexamethasone) was referred for evaluation of 3 months of hematochezia. He reported two to three loose bowel movements per day (Bristol type 5–6) with mixed blood; polyethylene glycol produced looser stools without reducing bleeding. He denied abdominal pain, weight loss, rashes, arthritis, oral or perianal lesions. He was intermittently neutropenic and consistently lymphopenic. On examination his abdomen was soft and nontender; a small nonbleeding external hemorrhoid was noted. Stool studies, including culture and PCR for Clostridioides difficile, cytomegalovirus, and adenovirus, were negative. Colonoscopy showed multiple semisessile, nonbleeding 1–5 mm polyps in the rectum and sigmoid colon with surrounding erythematous, eroded mucosa; the rest of the colon appeared normal. Histologic examination of the polyps revealed eroded surface mucosa with reactive hyperplastic glands and marked expansion of the lamina propria by a dense mixed inflammatory infiltrate predominantly composed of pale histiocytes with vacuolated cytoplasm admixed with eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes. The histiocytes contained numerous basophilic spherical and targetoid inclusions that were strongly positive on von Kossa and periodic acid–Schiff stains. Additional fungal (Grocott–Gömöri’s methenamine silver) and acid-fast (Kinyoun) stains were negative for organisms.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma. The patient continued to deteriorate, became comatose, and died approximately four weeks after admission.

Palpation revealed a firm, mobile, non-tender mass approximately 4 cm in diameter, located deep in the left buccal space and extending below the zygomatic arch; no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Intraorally, there was a bulge of the left buccal mucosa; palpation confirmed a well-defined, firm, non-tender mass. An orthopantomogram showed no bony destruction of the mandible or maxilla, with only a healed post-extraction socket in the region of tooth 36. Ultrasonography of the left cheek demonstrated a discrete, well-demarcated, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 2.6 × 2.0 cm, overlying the parotid gland, with no increase in internal vascular flow or calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed a well-bordered, slightly enhancing soft-tissue tumor measuring 2.7 × 3.7 × 4.0 cm in the left buccal space, indenting but not destroying adjacent bones (including the posterior maxillary sinus wall, medial pterygoid, masseter, and temporal muscle), and extending into the temporal space; the mass was supplied by branches of the left buccal artery. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded a hypocellular sample with erythrocytes, histiocytes, and neutrophils but showed “no signs of malignancy.” An intraoral incisional biopsy demonstrated “wide fibroblast proliferation, extremely similar to a fibroma.”

Her medical history was notable for irritable bowel syndrome and diet-controlled gluten intolerance; she denied tobacco and alcohol use. cases.vignette: A 7-year-old girl presented with a 2-year history of an enlarging, intermittently painful, purplish lump in her left ear canal. Approximately 18 months earlier, she had developed cracking and pus-filled sores at the site and received antibiotics and analgesics before referral. On examination, there was a 3.5 × 2.5 cm purplish-red mass in the left external ear canal, with an irregular, friable surface and bleeding on minimal contact. Contrast-enhanced CT of the mastoids showed a lobulated mass in the cutis and subcutis of the left auricle extending into the external acoustic canal and into the left parotid space, with bilateral level II–IV cervical lymph nodes up to 0.6 cm in diameter. CT angiography demonstrated marked vascularity of the mass, supplied by branches of the left superficial temporal and posterior auricular arteries. Incisional biopsy revealed atypical cells and granulomatous inflammation, leading to a provisional diagnosis of an auricular malignant tumor without a clear histopathological subtype.

cases.vignette:
A 53-year-old Hispanic man with no prior comorbidities presented with a two-week history of recurrent cough, nonmassive hemoptysis, and central chest pain. One month earlier, he had mild COVID-19 not requiring hospitalization. He also reported fatigue, myalgias, and anorexia but denied fever, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he was tachycardic but in no acute distress; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (25.56×10^3/μL), blood urea nitrogen 107 mg/dL, creatinine 5.8 mg/dL (baseline unknown), mild transaminitis, hyponatremia, and hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis and urine indices were ordered.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral scattered infiltrates with a denser consolidation in the right upper lobe. Noncontrast chest CT revealed multiple peripheral patchy consolidations in both lungs, some cavitating. These findings were interpreted as multifocal pneumonia.

He received intravenous azithromycin and ceftriaxone, intravenous bicarbonate, and emergent hemodialysis for acute kidney injury. Blood, sputum, and urine cultures were obtained, and PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. Postoperatively, he was found to have HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 191 000 copies/mL. Serum toxoplasma IgG was elevated, and CSF studies showed 48 cells/µL (97% lymphocytes) with positive toxoplasma IgG and DNA-PCR for Toxoplasma gondii (286 copies/mL). Other CSF studies, including fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and AFB smear/culture, were negative. Histopathologic examination of the brain tissue revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites. He was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and started on antiretroviral therapy; empiric antibiotics for bacterial abscess were discontinued. Two weeks after discharge, he returned with fever to 39.6 °C, generalized weakness, and a 1-day history of productive cough. Chest radiograph showed a new left upper lobe opacification with diffuse reticulonodular interstitial prominence. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions. His respiratory status worsened, and intubation was planned pending further diagnostic evaluation.

cases.vignette: A 60‐year‐old tailor with no significant medical history presented with a 3‐year history of macerated skin between his toes. He complained of a painful, fissured ulcer at the base of the fourth interdigital space of the right foot, which had been progressively enlarging over the past 18 months. He had received multiple antifungal regimens—including topical sertaconazole for 6 weeks and oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 weeks—without improvement. cases.vignette: A 47-year-old man was referred for mechanical circulatory support for severe cardiogenic shock with multiorgan failure of unknown cause. One day earlier, he had undergone excision of a benign thyroglossal duct cyst, during which he experienced recurrent hypertensive episodes. After extubation, he developed profound hypotension and pulmonary oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severely impaired left ventricular (LV) systolic function. Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of relevant coronary artery disease, and toxicological screening was negative. His medical history included chronic polyarthritis and treated arterial hypertension. On transfer, he was invasively ventilated (PaO2/FiO2 30 mmHg), receiving norepinephrine at 2.5 µg/kg/min. Blood pressure was 75/49 mmHg, heart rate 180 b.p.m., with bilateral rales and basal dullness on chest percussion. He experienced pulseless electrical activity requiring 5 minutes of resuscitation. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated akinesia of all basal and mid LV segments with preserved apical contraction (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%); right ventricular function was preserved (TAPSE 17 mm). On the basis of these findings, reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy was suspected. A percutaneous LV assist device (Impella CP®) was implanted immediately. Endomyocardial biopsy revealed moderate chronically active myocarditis with diffuse interstitial remodelling, and PCR testing showed no evidence of acute or persistent myocardial infection.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. She was in good general condition, weighed 5 kg, had an oxygen saturation of 80%, and showed no signs of respiratory distress. Her medications included furosemide and spironolactone. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. Approximately 12 hours after the procedure, the patient developed clonic movements of the left upper limb and persistent sucking motions. A noncontrast head CT obtained after this first seizure showed a slight diffuse increase in cortical density predominantly in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and, to a lesser extent, in the left parietal and occipital lobes; there was no mass effect, hemorrhage, or other intracranial abnormality.

cases.vignette:
A 42-year-old man with 30 pack-years of smoking, cannabis use, alcohol dependence, and the use of herbal products for addiction cessation presented with a 3-day history of acute urinary retention, hematemesis, and progressive neurological deficits. On day 3, he developed marked paraparesis of the lower limbs (muscle strength 2/5), was unable to stand or walk, and had hyperreflexia with sustained clonus in the lower extremities. Sensory function—including proprioception, light touch, and vibration—was normal. He also had hypertonic sphincters and hyperalgesia. Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal. He was febrile, and his condition deteriorated into respiratory distress requiring intubation and sedation.

Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid without albuminocytologic dissociation: glucose 0.49 g/L, protein 0.20 g/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, 14 white blood cells (70% lymphocytes), and 14 red blood cells per mm³; cultures were sterile. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL falling to 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (18 350 cells/μL), platelet counts fluctuating between 98 000 and 136 000 cells/μL, hyponatremia corrected from 117.5 mEq/L to 146 mEq/L over 8 days, potassium levels between 5.5 and 4.6 mEq/L, elevated AST (134 U/L) and ALT (65.9 U/L), and CRP 128.8–131.2 mg/L. Renal function remained normal.

Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral, symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and periaqueductal regions, dorsomedial thalami, medial temporal lobes, caudate nuclei, and brainstem, with diffusion restriction and low ADC values. Spinal MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensities throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord. A follow-up MRI a few days later revealed worsening of these lesions, new involvement of the lenticular nuclei, and patchy contrast enhancement in the cerebral peduncles, superior cerebellar peduncles, superior colliculi, right pons, and bilateral medulla. There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed lymphadenopathy in the bilateral cervical and axillary regions, left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and marked peri- and pararenal soft-tissue infiltration.

Laboratory studies showed urea 18.8 mmol/L, creatinine 141 µmol/L, lipase 182 U/L, myoglobin 108 ng/mL, ferritin >40 000 µg/L, vitamin B12 <111 pmol/L, normal fibrinogen, and triglycerides. Viral serologies were negative. Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, WBC 1.7×10^3/µL, ANC 0.9×10^3/µL, platelets 2×10^3/µL. Head CT showed bilateral subdural hemorrhages without midline shift. Whole-body CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusion, extensive pulmonary consolidation, thrombosis of the celiac artery with splenic infarction, mild hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly with infarction. Initial peripheral smear showed very few atypical cells; a repeat smear revealed marked leukopenia and 13% abnormal blastoid cells of medium size with fine nuclear chromatin, unevenly distributed coarse basophilic granules, and occasional bilobed nuclei. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with 26% immature metachromatic blasts—cells with eccentric nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and coarse giant granules—as well as some agranular high N/C blasts and spindle-shaped cells. There was trilineage dysplasia with megaloblastic changes in granulocytes and erythroid precursors, dysplastic megakaryocytes, and frequent mitoses. Both histiocytes and the atypical cells demonstrated erythrophagocytosis.

cases.vignette: A 74-year-old Caucasian woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed in 2006, complex karyotype with TP53 mutation and trisomy 12) was receiving zanubrutinib and subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement for hypogammaglobulinemia. In May 2022 she was hospitalized for pulmonary sepsis, treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and caspofungin, with resolution. One month later, she developed grade 4 neutropenia (<500/μL) for over 15 days and a febrile peak. Starting 15 June, tender, warm, erythematous nodular skin lesions appeared on the lower limbs and then the upper limbs; the lesions progressed to central ulceration with a necrotic core. On 25 June, zanubrutinib was discontinued and oral itraconazole was begun after a 5 mm punch biopsy of a left-thigh lesion. Histopathological examination (HE, Giemsa, GMS, PAS, and Gram stains) showed severe diffuse lympho-monocytic inflammation with minimal necrosis, angioinvasive microbial structures, thrombosed small vessels, and sparse hyphal mats with sporangial-type cells. Within vessels, thin-walled (5–15 μm), pauciseptate hyphae with minimal branching were seen, along with numerous thick-walled ovoid sporangia (5–20 μm) that stained strongly with PAS, GMS, and Giemsa. Only a presumptive diagnosis of deep cutaneous fungal infection was made at this time.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 9-year-old boy presented with a 3-month history of a painless swelling in the right upper posterior tooth region that had grown progressively, causing facial asymmetry. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. Examination revealed a 4.0×3.5 cm diffuse, well-defined, hard, nontender swelling on the right middle third of the face, extending from 1 cm below the infraorbital margin to the inferior border of the mandible and from the ala of the nose posteriorly to the anterior border of the ramus. The overlying skin was normal. Intraorally, there was a 4.0×3.0 cm ovoid, hard, nontender swelling in the right buccal vestibule with buccal cortical expansion and slight palatal expansion but no mucosal changes. A provisional clinical diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma was made, with fibrous dysplasia as a consideration. Panoramic and periapical radiographs showed a ground-glass trabecular pattern with radiolucency around the roots of deciduous teeth and erupting premolars. A maxillary occlusal film demonstrated increased radiopacity, buccal cortical expansion, and a ground-glass appearance without palatal involvement. Cone-beam CT revealed expansion of the buccal and palatal cortical plates, involvement of more than half of the right maxillary sinus, a well-defined margin, and a ground-glass internal pattern. Based on these images, a radiological diagnosis of juvenile ossifying fibroma of the right posterior maxilla was made, with fibrous dysplasia considered less likely because “the margin of the swelling was well-defined and well demarcated from the surrounding areas which was very much unlike FD whose margin is ill-defined and merges with the surrounding areas.”

A 38-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hypertension first noted at age 24 during pregnancy and again at age 38 after a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She had been diagnosed with splenomegaly of unknown cause at age 21; her younger brother had a similar finding. A 45-year-old woman was admitted to an acute psychiatric hospital with depressed mood, suicidal ideation, and auditory hallucinations. She had been discharged five days earlier from another facility and had 18 emergency department visits in the prior year. Her psychiatric history included benzodiazepine use disorder, opiate use disorder, borderline personality disorder, and major depressive disorder. Home medications were clonazepam, clonidine, buprenorphine–naloxone, fluoxetine, gabapentin, and trazodone. She was unemployed, homeless, and without family support.

During the admission, she exhibited:
- Catatonia-like signs: flat affect with psychomotor retardation and fluctuating mutism; complete lack of social contact; twitching, eye grimacing, and shoulder shrugging; posturing and immobility; diaphoresis.
- Psychotic signs: mouthing words and seemingly responding to internal stimuli; thought blocking; reported auditory hallucinations.
- Seizure-like behavior: episodes of head jerking with eye fluttering without tongue biting; remained conversant; benign neurologic examination.

Clues suggesting volitional behavior included selective acceptance of benzodiazepines and gabapentin while refusing other medications, eating all meals despite “stupor,” abruptly lapsing into and out of catatonia-like and psychotic behaviors depending on the topic of conversation, purposeful movements to obtain lorazepam after seizures, and evidence of self‐induced urinary incontinence during one episode.

A regional catatonia specialist evaluated her and noted that she was unlikely to have catatonia. Repeated lorazepam challenge tests had limited effect on her behaviors and appeared to reinforce them.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3. At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

cases.vignette: A 62-year-old woman with IgG kappa plasma cell myeloma (Durie-Salmon IIA, R-ISS II), previously treated with multiple chemotherapy regimens, two autologous stem-cell transplants, thalidomide maintenance, and focal bone radiotherapy, underwent routine surveillance imaging. She was asymptomatic with stable vital signs and no hepatosplenomegaly on examination. Liver function tests, including ALT, AST, ALP, GGTP, and bilirubin, were within normal limits. On PET/CT, a 35 mm lesion in the right hepatic lobe showed an SUVmax of 6.1. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a 17 mm lesion in segment VI with moderately increased T2 signal, decreased T1 signal, weak heterogeneous contrast enhancement, and restricted diffusion, favoring a non-characteristic malignant lesion. Serial imaging over subsequent months showed a decrease in lesion size to 10 mm, followed by enlargement to 57 × 46 mm. Given these findings, a percutaneous liver biopsy was planned to establish a definitive diagnosis.

cases.vignette: A man in his 50s with a 12-year history of recurrent follicular lymphoma presented with a subacute, multifocal, pruritic, painful eruption that began on the abdomen and then involved the scalp, groin, and extremities. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. His medications included oxycodone, duvelisib (a PI3K inhibitor), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, all started 14 months earlier for lymphoma management. On examination, there were well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the abdomen, axillae, and inguinal folds; scattered erythematous scaly papules and plaques on the scalp, extremities, and hands; and confluent erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with plate-like scales on the plantar feet. A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with dysphagia and was diagnosed with T3N0M0 esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. On day 60, salvage reconstruction with a free jejunal autograft and pectoralis major muscle flap coverage was performed.

Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

cases.vignette: A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face. Five years earlier, he had developed slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area that were misdiagnosed as severe eczema and treated with multiple courses of oral prednisolone and cyclosporine without improvement. On examination, there were confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles, with sparing of the nails and scalp. Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present; there was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Three skin punch biopsies (lower back, left buttock, right upper extremity) demonstrated epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7; CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 50-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance. He reported no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss and had no history of smoking or known malignancy. On examination, he had full strength throughout all extremities but had decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward. He exhibited four beats of clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression. CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, and laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. Given his rapidly progressive neurological decline, the decision was made to proceed urgently with surgical decompression, spinal stabilization, and tissue diagnosis.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of abnormal behavior, decreased concentration, and postural instability. She had a history of insomnia and irritable bowel syndrome and was taking vitamin D3, vitamin K, manganese, and activated charcoal. She and her parents denied other medications. She had been started on lorazepam by her general practitioner without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Teeth had a greyish discoloration. Neurologic exam showed confusion, impaired attention, and disorientation. Muscle tone and strength were normal; coordination, sensation, and cranial nerves were intact; there were no pyramidal signs.

While in the emergency department, she became more somnolent and developed frequent myoclonic jerks. Laboratory tests including CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, CRP, vitamin B12, and folate were normal; syphilis and HIV tests were negative. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed protein 47 mg/dL (15–45) and 10 WBC/μL (<5). Empiric IV acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started for possible infectious encephalitis.

On the neurology service, she remained moderately drowsy with exuberant generalized myoclonus at rest and on action. EEG revealed generalized background slowing without focal or periodic features. Brain MRI on hospital day 5 was normal. She clinically worsened despite antivirals and antibiotics, so intravenous immunoglobulin was given empirically for presumed autoimmune encephalitis. A trial of levetiracetam 1000 mg/day failed to improve the myoclonus.

cases.vignette: A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes presented with several days of urinary retention and inability to ambulate in the setting of a 1-year history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and a 100-lb unintentional weight loss. Her weakness began in the proximal left leg, gradually involved the right leg and both hands, and was accompanied by worsening numbness and tingling in her feet; she became wheelchair-dependent within 6 months. She denied pain, flank pain, hematuria, fevers, visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulty. On examination, she was alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact. She had bilateral weakness of hip flexors, knee flexors, knee extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles, with atrophy of the hands and thighs. Sensation to light touch was reduced in the feet, with slight impairment of vibration and proprioception. Reflexes were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent at the knees and ankles; plantar responses were flexor. Bladder catheterization yielded 1.8 L of retained urine. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; sodium 117 mmol/L; chloride 87 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 0.89 mg/dL; creatinine 25 mg/dL. Urine was negative for protein or bacteria. CSF analysis revealed protein 175 mg/dL, glucose 105 mg/dL, 1 WBC, 0 RBC; CSF cytology was negative for malignancy. Lyme serology, autoimmune panel, and a comprehensive paraneoplastic antibody panel were negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.5 g/dL. On hospital day 4, electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated decreased amplitudes in motor and sensory nerves, slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, and absent sensory responses, suggesting a chronic length-dependent sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with superimposed chronic lumbosacral plexopathy. MRI of the pelvis showed bilateral femoral nerve enlargement without enhancement.

cases.vignette: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A recent exercise stress test induced angina at 50 W without ECG changes. On admission, he appeared anxious; the physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A 27-year-old man with a history of a 5 mm‐thick melanoma on his posterior neck treated six years earlier by wide local excision (no sentinel lymph node biopsy, no adjuvant therapy) presented with hemoptysis and dyspnea. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was notable only for scattered breath sounds without stridor. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest revealed a 3.1 × 2.7 × 3.6 cm mass in the right lower lobe. Endobronchial ultrasound–guided fine-needle aspiration of the lung lesion demonstrated a malignant small round blue cell tumor. Molecular studies were negative for an EWSR1 translocation but otherwise were interpreted as consistent with Ewing sarcoma/primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET). 

Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT showed an FDG-avid right lower lobe mass and an intensely FDG-avid, partially calcified 4.1 × 2.3 × 2.8 cm expansile lesion within the right hyoid bone. Ultrasound–guided core needle biopsy of the hyoid lesion was nondiagnostic, yielding only rare atypical epithelial cells amidst lymphocytes.

A multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board concluded that the hyoid lesion most likely represented a synchronous primary bone tumor (e.g., plasmacytoma, chondrosarcoma, or osteosarcoma). Given his pulmonary symptoms and the potential for chemotherapy to treat both lesions, he received 14 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and etoposide (VCD/IE). 

Mid-treatment PET/CT demonstrated a substantial decrease in size and complete metabolic response of the lung mass but development of right neck adenopathy and interval growth of the hyoid bone lesion, suggesting a distinct pathology.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 54-year-old man with glioblastoma treated by surgical resection began a clinical trial with M7824 (a bifunctional fusion protein targeting PD-L1 and TGF-β). Four weeks after initiation of M7824, he presented with a severely pruritic, nontender, erythematous papular and macular eruption on his back, bilateral ankles, and upper extremities. He was not receiving any other new medications. The oncology team initially classified the eruption as a grade I rash and prescribed hydrocortisone 1% cream and oral diphenhydramine, but the rash and pruritus progressed. One month later, the rash reached grade II severity, and doxycycline was started for a suspected acneiform eruption. On dermatologic evaluation, the consensus was that the eruption represented a drug reaction to M7824. Laboratory evaluation showed no elevations in liver enzymes, no eosinophilia, and no lymphadenopathy. The patient was treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment and hydroxyzine, but over the following two weeks the rash progressed to grade III with worsening pruritus. M7824 infusions were held, and prednisone at 40 mg per day was initiated according to guidelines, but his symptoms failed to improve.

A 40-year-old man presented with a painful nodule on the lower part of his right leg. He reported that the lesion had been stable in size and painless for 4 years but had enlarged and become tender over the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma or personal or family history of malignancy.

Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, fasting blood sugar, liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV were negative.

On light microscopy, the dermal tumor extended into the superficial subcutis and was composed of nests and fascicles of spindle-shaped to epithelioid cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli within a collagenous stroma. Mitotic figures, including atypical forms, measured 7–8 per 10 high-power fields. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal. Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

cases.vignette:
A 67-year-old woman with a 4-day history of fever and cough was admitted to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR. Five days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, prompting intubation and transfer to the ICU. Her comorbidities included diabetes mellitus with dialysis-dependent nephropathy, angina, prior gastric cancer resection, and spinal‐canal stenosis; she was on an antiplatelet agent.  
On arrival: temperature 34 °C; blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; heart rate 102 beats/min; GCS E1VtM1 under deep sedation. Arterial blood gas (on pressure‐control ventilation: PEEP 8 cmH₂O, PiP 25 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.5) showed pH 7.309, PaCO₂ 41.5 mmHg, PaO₂ 78.2 mmHg.

cases.vignette: A 50-year-old woman with hypertension and COPD first presented 5 months before admission with lower abdominal pain and decreased bowel movements; she was diagnosed with constipation. One month later, she returned with left lower-quadrant pain and low-grade fevers and was treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for presumed diverticulitis. Symptoms partially improved, but she then had right upper-quadrant pain; abdominal CT was performed and incidentally revealed a confluent retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass encasing surrounding vessels. A HIDA scan confirmed cholecystitis, and she underwent cholecystectomy. One month after surgery, she had 5 days of progressively worsening, constant epigastric pain with nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anorexia, decreased urine output, and a 20-lb weight loss over 4 months. She denied fevers, chills, dysuria, or GI bleeding. On exam, blood pressure was 162/91 mmHg, pulse 79, and she had slight epigastric tenderness without guarding. Renal ultrasound demonstrated mild bilateral hydronephrosis, and postrenal obstruction was suspected. The following morning, a retrograde pyelogram showed bilateral hydronephrosis with extrinsic compression and medial deviation of the ureters, most prominently on the right. Ureteral stents were placed, relieving her obstruction, and her renal function subsequently returned to baseline.

cases.vignette: A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

cases.vignette: A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. He denied contact allergens, fever, or hyperhidrosis and had no prior history of atopic dermatitis, dermatophytosis, or hand eczema. On examination, he had scleral icterus and multiple dusky, thin plaques with a central collarette of scale on the face, neck, axillae, trunk, and extremities. On both hands and feet, there were hyperkeratotic plaques and deeply seated vesicles with a greenish-black hue, especially accentuated along the dermatoglyphic ridges. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. A punch biopsy of the right palm revealed psoriasiform epidermal acanthosis, intraepidermal spongiosis, hyperkeratosis with sparse perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, and a dilated eccrine duct containing amorphous pink material. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

A 30-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman was referred at 32 weeks’ gestation after an abnormal routine ultrasound. She had no significant medical history, no medication use, and no history of trauma. Previous prenatal care had been irregular.  
Transabdominal ultrasound showed bilateral ventriculomegaly with dilation of both frontal and occipital horns, irregular ventricular walls, multiple hyperechoic regions with indistinct margins within the ventricular lumens, and a roughened-appearing choroid plexus.  
Fetal Doppler ultrasound demonstrated normal middle cerebral artery perfusion.

cases.vignette: A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology. Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.

Neurological examination showed a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, imbalance, uncoordinated movements, bilateral nystagmus, and stage I bilateral papilledema. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no abnormalities. Brain MRI revealed an inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis measuring 40 × 31 × 29 mm, hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed an elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal.

cases.vignette: A 46-year-old Japanese woman with a history of epilepsy presented with redness and swelling of the right breast. On examination, there was erythema and swelling in the lower right breast. Ultrasound revealed a 54 × 41 × 31 mm low-echo mass with partially unclear margins in the outer right breast. Biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type), high grade, ER+, PgR–, HER2 3+, Ki67 70%. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased uptake in the right axilla, anterior mediastinum, left pleura, and liver, consistent with cT4dN3M1 stage IV breast cancer. She received four cycles of FEC chemotherapy, after which lesions nearly disappeared, and then trastuzumab plus pertuzumab with docetaxel, achieving a clinical complete response maintained for 23 months. Two years after treatment initiation, she developed a persistent headache. CT and MRI of the head revealed a 30-mm mass lesion in the right temporal lobe.
